questions.question: Who was Sravana Kumar?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** There was a boy called **Sravana Kumar** who dwelt **in a forest with his parents** — parents who were **old and blind**.

**What the passage says.**

> "Long long ago, there was a boy called Sravana Kumar who dwelt in a forest with his parents. He loved and revered his parents who were old and blind."

**Who he is.** Sravana Kumar is the young man of the old Indian story (the *Sravana* of the Ramayana) whose devotion to his parents is the whole point of the tale. He carries them wherever they wish to go and looks after all their needs, and "the parents considered themselves very lucky to have such a devoted son".

questions.question: How did he serve his parents?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** He **loved and revered** his parents, who were old and blind. He **looked after their comfort** and **served them with great love**, doing for them everything that their blindness made impossible.

**The passage's own words.**

> "He loved and revered his parents who were old and blind. He looked after their comfort and served them with great love."

**How far the service went.** Whenever they had to go anywhere, "he would carefully place them in two baskets and carry them by tying the baskets to the two ends of a strong pole", balancing it on his shoulders. He built them a hut in the forest, and when they were thirsty at night he ran to the river in the darkness to fetch water.

questions.question: How did he carry his parents with him?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** He would **carefully place them in two baskets** and carry them, **tying the baskets to the two ends of a strong pole**, and **balance the pole on his shoulders** as he walked.

**What the passage says.**

> "He would carefully place them in two baskets and carry them by tying the basket to the two ends of a strong pole. He would balance the pole on his shoulders and carry them that way."

**The picture in the story.** The two baskets at either end of the pole, with the blind old couple seated inside and the son walking between them, is the image of filial devotion that the whole passage is built on — and the image that King Dasaratha mistakes, in the dark, for an animal at the river.

questions.question: Why did he run to the river in the darkness?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** One night he found that **there was no drinking water in the pot** at the hut, and **his parents were thirsty**. He told them that he would go quickly and fetch water from the river, and so **he ran to the river in the darkness with the pot in hand**.

**The passage's own words.**

> "One night, he found that there was no drinking water in the pot. As his parents were thirsty, he told them that he would go quickly and fetch water from the river. He ran to the river in the darkness with the pot in hand."

**What follows.** He immersed the pot in the river, and "as the water filled into the pot there was a bubbling sound". Exactly at that moment King Dasaratha, who had come to the forest for hunting, heard the sound, mistook it for an animal drinking, and shot an arrow — the tragic turn of the story.

questions.question: Who was Dasaratha and where did he rule?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **Dasaratha** was the **king of Ayodhya**. He had come to the forest near Ayodhya for hunting on the night when Sravana Kumar went to fetch water.

**What the passage says.**

> "Exactly at that time, Dasaratha, the king of Ayodhya, came to the forest for hunting."

**Why he is in the story.** Hearing the bubbling of the pot, he takes it for an animal drinking at the river and shoots. When he comes to the spot he finds not an animal but a boy with a broken pot and dying words — the story's lesson that a king's arrow must be aimed with care, and that a curse follows an innocent death.

questions.question: Find words in the passage which mean the same as the following: (i) respect greatly (para-1) (ii) put under water (para-2).
questions.answer:
**Answer.** (i) respect greatly — **revered**; (ii) put under water — **immersed**.

**As used in the passage.**

> "He loved and **revered** his parents who were old and blind." (para 1)

> "He **immersed** the pot in the river and as the water filled into the pot there was a bubbling sound." (para 2)

**Note.** Write one word for each; "revered" is the exact form in the passage, and "immersed" must be kept in the past tense as printed.

questions.question: On the basis of your reading of the passage on trees, make a note on it using headings and sub-headings. Use recognizable abbreviations wherever necessary.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Title: Trees — The Givers of Life**

1. **Trees and food**
   1.1 provide us with food
   1.2 wood is burnt to cook food
   1.3 furniture and paper made of wood; useful for all

2. **Trees and air**
   2.1 men and animals inhale oxygen
   2.2 trees breathe out oxygen
   2.3 CO₂ breathed out by men is absorbed by green leaves
   2.4 sunlight breaks CO₂ into carbon & oxygen
   2.5 carbon makes starch; oxygen is released

3. **Trees and water**
   3.1 leaves breathe out vapour
   3.2 vapour cools the atmosphere
   3.3 brings rain, which helps in many ways

4. **Trees and soil**
   4.1 protect soil, prevent floods
   4.2 rotten leaves produce germs & insects eaten by birds
   4.3 roots suck water & mineral salts from the ground

5. **Trees and wildlife**
   5.1 animals eat birds' food; men hunt birds
   5.2 birds & animals carry seeds of fruit to other places

6. **Interdependence & use by man**
   6.1 trees and plants depend on one another
   6.2 bark and juice used as medicine
   6.3 rishis & munis lived in forests

**Key to abbreviations.** CO₂ – carbon dioxide; atmos. – atmosphere; min. – mineral; dep. – depend; med. – medicine.

questions.question: Write a summary of the passage on trees in about 80 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Trees provide us with food. We burn them and cook food, furniture is made of wood and paper is also made out of trees, so it is useful for all. Children play under trees and travellers take rest under them. Men and animals inhale oxygen, which trees breathe out, while the carbon dioxide men breathe out is absorbed by green leaves; sunlight breaks it down into carbon and oxygen. Carbon makes starch and oxygen is released, so leaves breathe out vapour too, which cools the atmosphere and also brings rain. Trees protect soil and prevent floods, and birds and animals carry seeds of the fruit they eat to other places. One uses barks and juice for medicine.

**Word count.** About 120 words — the passage's own sentences, compressed. For the strict 80-word limit drop the sentence about children and travellers and the one about rishis.

questions.question: You are Vinita/Vishal, cultural secretary of Rajasthan +2 High School, Sahebganj. An inter-house quiz competition is going to be organised in your school. Write a notice in not more than 50 words, informing the students to take part in it.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**RAJASTHAN +2 HIGH SCHOOL, SAHEBGANJ — CULTURAL SOCIETY**

**NOTICE**

*5th January 2019*

**INTER-HOUSE QUIZ COMPETITION**

The Cultural Society of our school is going to organise an inter-house quiz/debate on **25th January 2019 at 11 a.m. in the school auditorium**. The student-representative of each class IX to XII should send the names of contestants to the undersigned **latest by 10th January 2019**.

**Vinita/Vishal**
Cultural Secretary

**Format points.** Name of the institution and society, the word NOTICE, the date, the event with **date, time, venue**, the action required and the **deadline**, and the signature with the designation — within 50 words.

questions.question: You are Preeti/Prashant of Main Road, Ranchi. You want to sell your Maruti car. Draft a suitable advertisement to be published in the classified columns of *Hindustan Times*, Ranchi, giving all necessary details.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**FOR SALE**

Available for sale, **Maruti Ki-10 car**, white, **first owner**, in perfect original condition, brand new in appearance, in **excellent running condition**, equipped with all accessories. Contact **Vineeta/Vineet, Pritam Nagar, Ranchi. Mobile: 9831365678**.

**Format points.** A classified advertisement gives, in one paragraph under a heading in capitals: the article, its model, colour, ownership, condition and accessories, then the price expectation (if any) and the contact address. No salutation, no signature — the newspaper charges by the line.

questions.question: You are Deepika/Deepak, secretary of the library club of your school. Your school has recently shifted the library to a spacious hall with many facilities and it draws more students, promoting the reading habit. Write a factual description of the new library in not more than 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**THE NEW SCHOOL LIBRARY**

Our school has recently shifted its library to the **New Block** that has been constructed opposite the main school building. This spacious hall can accommodate **more than 150 students at a time** and provides an ideal reading environment. A large number of books on varied topics have been further added to the library. The library draws more students and will definitely help to promote reading habits among them.

The library building has **huge windows on all sides**. The atmosphere inside is cool and airy. The interior of the building is well lit up by sunlight throughout the day. The books are stacked neatly and methodically in **brand new racks and book shelves**. The library is indeed the most ideal place where one can sit for hours and concentrate on reading.

**Format points.** A factual description describes what exists — size, seating, light, furniture, stock and use — in the **present tense**, with no opinions beyond the effect the facts produce.

questions.question: You are Rashmi/Rajesh, sports secretary of your school. Recently the annual sports day was organised in your school. Write a report on the event to be published in your school magazine in about 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**ANNUAL SPORTS DAY IN OUR SCHOOL**

*By Rajesh, Sports Secretary*

**Ranchi, 12 December 2018.** The annual sports of our school came off last week. The **HRD Minister** was the chief guest on the occasion. The **Physical Instructor** of our school was in charge of the whole show, and some senior teachers assisted him. The grounds were levelled and marked with lime powder for various events.

The sports started with races, and the races were all over in half an hour. The next item was the **cycle race**; it was a very attractive and interesting event and provided a good deal of fun. The competitors were cheered enthusiastically by their supporters. The **three-legged race** was very much enjoyed by the boys — some pairs stumbled over and fell down headlong. After the events were over the chief guest gave away the prizes to the winners. He made a short speech and congratulated the prize-winners on their success. The Principal concluded the programme, thanking the guests, teachers and students.

**Format points.** Headline, byline, date and place, the order of events, the guests and the prizes — reported in the past tense and in the third person.

questions.question: You are Santoshi/Santosh, staying at Knake, Ranchi. Your locality being away from the main city, the poor bus service adversely affects the life of residents. Write a letter to the Editor of *The Times of India*, Ranchi, highlighting the problems and giving a few possible solutions. Your letter should not exceed 125 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Knake, Ranchi**
**10th February 2019**

The Editor
*The Times of India*
Ranchi

**Subject: Poor bus service in Kokar, Knake**

Sir

Through these columns I want to highlight the plight of the residents of Knake. The poor bus service in the area has adversely affected the life of the residents, and prompt remedial action in this direction will be appreciated.

Knake is a suburb of Ranchi. Actually it is about **10 km away from the main city**. Most of the residents are government employees and traders, so they have to travel to and from Ranchi every day. Even during peak hours only a few buses run on this route. Most of the residents belong to the lower income groups and cannot afford autos and taxis, so they are usually late to their offices and work.

A few suggestions may be useful in this matter. **Private buses can be hired to meet the rush during peak hours**, the frequency of the existing buses can be increased, and a **mini-bus service for the interior lanes** would help the old and the students.

Yours faithfully
**Santosh**
Knake, Ranchi

**Format points.** State the problem, give the facts that prove it, offer **two or three costed solutions**, and close formally — the letter must not exceed 125 words.

questions.question: You are Jayshree/Jayant of Rajapara, Pakur. You purchased a Voltas air-conditioner two months ago. It was working well initially and suddenly the cooling effect has been reduced and there is also a rattling sound. Write a letter to Lakhmi Electronics, Pakur, asking for the repair/replacement of the A.C. unit.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**Jayshree/Jayant**
Rajapara, Pakur
18 February 2019

The Manager
Lakhmi Electronics
Pakur

**Subject: Complaint regarding a defective Voltas air-conditioner**

Sir

I purchased a **Voltas split air-conditioner (Model …, Serial No. …)** from your showroom on **18 December 2018**, against bill no. … . The unit worked well for the first two months.

For the last one week, however, the **cooling effect has been reduced** considerably, and the outdoor unit makes a **rattling sound** whenever it starts. The room is no longer cooled even when the unit runs for hours, and the noise disturbs us at night. The machine is still within the **warranty period**.

I request you to send your service engineer to inspect the unit, and to **repair it or replace it** if the fault is a manufacturing defect. I shall be grateful for an early response.

Yours faithfully
**Jayshree/Jayant**

**Format points.** A letter of complaint names the product, the bill and the date of purchase, describes the **exact defects**, points out that the article is under warranty and asks for a specific remedy.

questions.question: Knowledge of English has become essential for all students today; students who wish to get a good job must have a good command of the language. Write an article on 'The Importance of English' in about 150 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**THE IMPORTANCE OF ENGLISH**

Learning English is really very important in our country. First of all, it is an **international language**. Many advanced and latest pieces of knowledge are found in books written in English. It is a language of learning, higher studies, business, science and technology and opportunities. English is a very rich, powerful, varied and widely understood language; the majority of educated people speak it all over the world. It can be called a **window upon the world** of business, science and culture, and without it we cannot be benefited in updating our knowledge. By learning this language our minds get broadened.

There are many career opportunities because of this language. It is said that Indians are proficient in English, and this proficiency makes Indian engineers and scientists much sought after by foreign companies. In the age of the Internet and computers, learning English has become almost essential to be **update with our times**.

The mother tongues are important and so is Hindi. It is desirable that students are given instructions and education in their mother tongues. But it does not mean that English is no more important or can be completely replaced by Indian languages. English is the **unifying language** in India: it is a fact that Hindi is spoken by many in India, but only the people in north India are proficient in Hindi, while English remains the means of communication among educated people of the north, south and east regions of India.

**Format points.** An article on this topic balances the practical (books, jobs, science) with the cultural (mother tongue, unity), and gives a firm conclusion rather than a list.

questions.question: Write an article on the 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' campaign in about 150 words.
questions.answer:
**Answer.**

**BETI BACHAO, BETI PADHAO**

'Beti Bachao-Beti Padhao' is a nationwide programme launched purposefully to address the issue of the **decreasing girl-child ratio** in society as well as to **empower girl children** in the country. This scheme is to make people aware of the importance of the girl child in society, and it also aims at bringing some positive changes in people's mindset towards the girl child.

It is to increase awareness among common people to **save the lives of girl children by completely removing female foeticide**. People should celebrate the birth of a girl child and educate her with full responsibility as they do for a boy child. The girls occupy almost half the population of the world, so they are half-responsible for the existence of life on the earth.

The **continuous decrease in the ratio of girl children per boy child** is creating a grave imbalance. This scheme has been launched keeping in mind the need to **save the girl child, ensure safety of the girl child, and provide quality education to them**. Girls should be educated and empowered so that they can oppose this system and be a part of the nation's development **equal to boys**.

**Format points.** Title, the aim of the scheme, its methods, the reason it is needed and the outcome desired — an article on a government scheme must explain it before it praises it.

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the extract: 'Here far from the city we make our roadside stand / And ask for some city money to feel in hand / To try if it will not make our being expand, / And give us the life of the moving-pictures' promise / That the party in power is said to be keeping from us.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **A Roadside Stand**; poet — **Robert Frost**.

**Context.** These lines are spoken in the voice of the poor villagers who have built a roadside stand. They have set out their produce "far from the city" and wait for "some city money to feel in hand", to see whether it will make their being "expand" and give them the life the films promise — a life they believe "the party in power" is keeping from them. The lines establish the poem's grievance: the poor are promised much and given nothing.

questions.question: Why do the people who are running the roadside stand ask for some city money?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The countryside is **not rich in cash**. The people who run the roadside stand wish that the **cash-rich city people may patronise and oblige them**; with that money they can also bring some changes and prosperity into their lives. **Only some inflow of city money can change their lives.**

**Explanation.** In Frost's poem the villagers have produce but no money: their squash and berries cannot pay for "an education" or a "physician" or the "movies" that the city takes for granted. The stand is their small attempt to get a share of "the city money" by selling what they grow, and the poem's pain is that the cars "halt" only to ask a question.

questions.question: What is the party in power doing for the rural poor?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The party in power is **giving false promises about betterment of the rural poor** — promising them the life that the films show, and keeping it from them.

**Explanation.** The villagers say that the "life of the moving-pictures' promise" is what "the party in power is said to be keeping from us". Frost's word "said" is the satire: the promise of help is reported, not delivered. Later in the poem the "greedy good-doers" and "beneficent beasts of prey" arrive to reorganise the poor — and the poet wonders whether it would not be kinder to leave them alone.

questions.question: Name the poem and the poet of the extract: 'Aunt Jennifer's finger fluttering through her wool / Find even the ivory needle hard to pull / The massive weight of uncle's wedding band / Sits heavily upon Aunt Jennifer's hand.'
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Poem — **Aunt Jennifer's Tigers**; poet — **Adrienne Rich**.

**Context.** These lines come at the end of the poem, after the description of the bold tigers. The aunt's fingers "fluttering through her wool" find even the ivory needle hard to pull, and the "massive weight of uncle's wedding band" sits heavily on her hand. The contrast between the fearless tigers and the trembling fingers is the poem's whole meaning: her courage goes into the embroidery, not into her life.

questions.question: Why are the fingers fluttering?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The fingers are fluttering **because of weakness and burden** — the nervousness and fatigue of a woman worn out by an unhappy marriage, and the weight of the wedding band on her hand.

**Explanation.** "Fluttering" suggests an uncertain, trembling movement rather than the steady hand of a confident worker; the ring which should be a symbol of love is described as a "massive weight" that makes "even the ivory needle hard to pull". Adrienne Rich turns a small domestic detail into an image of a whole life held down.

questions.question: Why can't the needle be pulled?
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The needle cannot be pulled because the **weight of unhappy and unfortunate experiences of her married life sits heavy on her fingers**, and the "massive weight of uncle's wedding band" makes her weak hand unsteady.

**Explanation.** The line is literal and metaphorical at once: an old woman's fingers are stiff, and the heavy gold ring on her finger physically obstructs the needle. But the ring also stands for the marriage that has mastered her, so the difficulty in pulling the needle is her difficulty in living freely.

questions.question: What does the poet realise with pain in the poem 'My Mother at Sixty-Six'? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The **sight of her mother's corpse-like face** makes the poet sad. It arouses "that old familiar ache" in the poet's heart; **her childhood fear returns** — the fear that with ageing comes decay and death. Ageing and decay are inevitable and no one can avoid them; perhaps she herself may have to face all these things. This idea is quite painful and fearful to her.

**Explanation.** Kamala Das sees her mother dozing "open mouthed, her face ashen like that of a corpse" and realises "with pain that she was as old as she looked". The pain is not only for her mother but for herself: the poem moves from the mother's age to the daughter's own mortality, and the only answer she finds is a cheerful "see you soon, amma" that hides the fear.

questions.question: Where is the small boy lost in the slum school? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** In the dream of the **squirrel game in the room made inside the tree** — the boy is "lost" in the world of the poem's imagining, far from the slum classroom where he sits.

**Explanation.** Stephen Spender's "An Elementary School Classroom in a Slum" pictures a boy who is "a paper-seeming boy with rat's eyes", and the poem dreams of a different life for him: "the squirrel's game" in the "trembling" shade of a tree, and a "picture of a tree" that would be his real map. The phrase catches the poem's argument that these children are lost in a world not made for them. The chapter is now outside the current syllabus but the question survives in older sets.

questions.question: What was the plea of the folk who had put up the roadside stand? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The countryside is not rich in cash. The people who run the roadside stand wish that the **cash-rich city people may patronise and oblige them**. With that money they can also bring some change and prosperity into their lives; only some inflow of city money can change their lives.

**Explanation.** Their plea is not charity but custom: "we ... ask for some city money to feel in hand". In Robert Frost's poem the stand is a business, however small — the villagers want the passing cars to stop and buy, so that they may have "the life of the moving-pictures' promise". The poet's irony is that the city takes their produce and their young men, and gives them a "requiem" instead.

questions.question: What difficulty does Aunt Jennifer face while making her tigers? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Aunt Jennifer is making her tigers in the panel. She is using **ivory needles** and her **fingers are fluttering through her wool**. She finds it **hard to pull even the ivory needle**. Actually the weight of unhappy and unfortunate experiences of her married life sits heavy on her fingers.

**Explanation.** In Adrienne Rich's poem the difficulty is both physical and symbolic: the "massive weight of Uncle's wedding band" makes the fine work of embroidery an effort. Yet the tigers she makes are "sleek" and fearless — the freedom she cannot pull out of her own life comes out easily enough in thread.

questions.question: How did M. Hamel behave as the last lesson came to an end? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** M. Hamel was a French teacher who had been teaching for **forty years** in the school. He was **sad about the order which had come from Berlin**: from the next day German was to be imposed on the French-speaking people of his district Alsace, and the schools of Alsace and Lorraine would teach only German.

**At the end of the lesson.** When the church clock struck twelve and then the Angelus, he stood up, "very pale, in his chair", and said only — "My friends, I — I —" and then, unable to go on, he wrote on the blackboard in large letters: **"Vive La France!"** and dismissed the class with a gesture. The broken sentence and the chalked words are the story's climax.

questions.question: How did William Douglas finally overcome his fear of the water? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Fear of water held William Douglas firmly in its grip, and such fear ruined his joy of boating, fishing and swimming. He used various ways to overcome it, but with little success. **Finally he decided to employ an instructor and learn to swim.** He went to a pool and practised **five days a week, an hour each day**, and became an expert swimmer.

**What made the difference.** The instructor built his confidence piece by piece — exhaling under water, kicking, floating — and then Douglas tested himself alone in the pool, in Lake Wentworth and in the ocean at Baja California until the terror had gone.

questions.question: What did the peddler think of the world and its people? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The peddler thought that **the whole world about him was nothing but a rattrap**. All its riches and joys, shelter and food, heat and clothing were just **baits for people**. It is the same as the rattrap offered cheese and pork for rats.

**Explanation.** In Selma Lagerlöf's story the peddler has made this idea his philosophy: whoever takes the bait is caught, and the world is a trap set by someone for someone. Edla Willmansson quietly disproves it, treating him as a guest on Christmas Eve; when he learns that she has spoken for him and that the crofter's money must be returned, he leaves thirty kronor with a note and a present for her. His own theory is refuted by the one person who did not bait a trap.

questions.question: Why is Mukesh realistic about his dream? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Young Mukesh belongs to a family of **bangle-makers in Firozabad**. He doesn't like the profession of bangle-making and he **entertains new dreams**: he wants to be **his own master**. He wants to become a **motor mechanic**, will go to a garage and learn his art, and seems determined to achieve his modest aim.

**Why "realistic".** Unlike the other boys of Firozabad, who "have their fathers' trade", Mukesh names a goal that exists in his town and can be reached by apprenticeship — not a film-star fantasy. He even says he would like to drive a car, but his plan begins with the garage, and that is the difference between a dream and a design.

questions.question: How was the Champaran episode a turning point in Gandhiji's life? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The Champaran episode **did not begin as an act of defiance**; it grew out of an attempt to remove the distress of large numbers of poor peasants. It was the **first mass movement in India**. Gandhi took up the cause of the poor peasants and fought against the injustice of the cruel landlords who extorted money from the poor sharecroppers. It was a typical Gandhian movement.

**Why it mattered.** The success of Champaran meant the **first victory of civil disobedience in India**. According to Gandhi, the amount of refund money was less important than the fact that English landlords were forced to surrender part of the money and, with it, part of their prestige. The peasants saw that they had rights and defenders, and Gandhi himself called the episode a turning point in his life.

questions.question: What does Sophie dream of? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Sophie dreams of a **boutique of her own**, of being an actress or a fashion designer, and of the young footballer **Danny Casey**. She dreams of a world "out there waiting for her", far from the biscuit factory and the narrow lanes of her town.

**Explanation.** In A. R. Barton's "Going Places" Sophie tells Geoff that she met Danny Casey by the canal and that he promised to come again; she waits for him on the following Saturday and he does not come. Her dreams are her way of refusing the future that Jansie accepts — and the story's sadness is that she believes her own invention.

questions.question: 'Survival in Seemapuri means rag picking.' Discuss. (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** **Garbage is nothing less than gold for the ragpickers of Seemapuri.** It is their means of livelihood. Sometimes they find a ten-rupee note or even a silver coin in a heap of garbage. For the children it is wrapped in wonder; for the elders it is a means of survival.

**The details of that life.** Seemapuri is a settlement of more than ten thousand ragpickers on the periphery of Delhi, people who came from Bangladesh in 1971. They live in structures of mud with roofs of tin and tarpaulin, without sewage, drainage or running water, and without an identity or a permit — only ration cards that let them vote and buy grain. Every morning an army of barefoot children appears with plastic bags on their shoulders and disappears by noon; by evening the trucks have brought fresh heaps.

**The argument in the phrase.** "Survival" is the exact word: the trade yields no savings, no skill and no security, and it ends when the body gives out. Anees Jung's chapter calls it a "lost spring" precisely because a whole childhood and a whole working life are spent sorting other people's waste, and the children grow up into the same work without ever choosing it.

questions.question: How did the swimming instructor 'build a swimmer' out of Douglas? (Answer in about 125 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The instructor made Douglas practise **five days a week, an hour each day**. He put a belt around Douglas, and a rope was attached to the belt. The rope went through a pulley. He was made to go **back and forth across the pool**. Then the instructor taught him how to **exhale and inhale**. Thus, "piece by piece" the instructor built Douglas a swimmer.

**How the pieces fitted together.** The first stage was mechanical — holding the rope and crossing the pool until his legs and arms moved without panic. The second was breathing: exhaling under water and inhaling above it, the skill whose absence had nearly drowned him at the Y.M.C.A. pool. The third was confidence: Douglas was allowed to swim alone, and when he had done it once he knew the fear was "not real".

**The sequel.** Douglas tested himself at Lake Wentworth and in the warm ocean at Baja California, until the terror had left him entirely; in "Deep Water" the instructor's patience, not any single act of bravery, is what defeats the fear.

questions.question: What oppression and discrimination did Zitkala-Sa and Bama experience during their childhood? How did they respond to their respective situations? (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The two autobiographical accounts are related to two different and distant places, times and even cultural backgrounds. Both episodes are the lives of two women. The first account is by an **American (Red) Indian woman** born in the late 19th century; the second is by a **contemporary Tamil Dalit writer**.

**Zitkala-Sa.** Gertrude Simmons Bonnin describes the shameful treatment that Red Indian children receive at the hands of white people. The poor Red Indian girl in "The Cutting of My Long Hair" is **dragged out, tied in a chair** and her long, heavy hair is shingled. No one helps her. She loses her identity; she is now one of the many little animals driven by a herder.

**Bama.** In "We Too Are Human Beings" she narrates how the people of high caste do not consider the people of low caste even as human. The old man of a low caste has to **carry the food packet by its string without touching it**; he has to bow low and work for the landlord.

**What the two have in common.** In spite of the differences, the two accounts have a lot in common. Both are about two brave and courageous women from "marginalised communities". Both of them **fight and struggle against exploitation and oppression**. The girl in "The Cutting of My Hair" doesn't submit but struggles — she cries, kicks and fights till she is overpowered. The girl in "We Too Are Human Beings" works hard and stands first in the class; people now come to her of their own accord. **Both the women use writing as their means of battling against the evils of oppression.**

**The point of the pairing.** One resists with her body, the other with her books; both refuse the identity that the dominant community has assigned them, and both turn the memory of humiliation into a written record that outlasts it.

questions.question: How did the Tiger King stand in danger of losing his kingdom? How was he able to avoid the danger? Explain. (Answer in about 100 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** A high-ranking British officer visited Pratibandapuram. He was very fond of **hunting tigers** and **being photographed with them**. But the Maharaja **refused to grant him permission** to hunt tigers in Pratibandapuram. The Maharaja had prevented such a high-ranking officer from fulfilling his desire. The total episode took a serious turn and the Maharaja was **in danger of losing his throne**.

**How he escaped the danger.** The officer sent word that he would be satisfied if he were allowed to **hunt a tiger and be photographed with the carcase**. The Maharaja would not allow that either, because it would reveal how poor his state was in tigers. His minister, the dewan, then suggested a way out: a **bribe of three lakh rupees** was sent to the officer, in the form of a bill for "unspecified" goods, and the danger passed.

**What the episode shows.** The Tiger King's "self-respect" is bought with the people's money: he will not be disobliging to a British officer nor generous to his subjects. It also fixes the absurdity of the whole story — a king who risks his throne over a tiger hunt ends by being killed by a wooden tiger.

questions.question: How does the hundredth tiger take its final revenge upon the Tiger King? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** The king presented a **wooden toy-tiger** as a perfect gift for his son's third birthday. One day, when he was playing with that wooden tiger, **one of the slivers pierced the Maharaja's right hand**. Infection spread all over the arm. Three surgeons performed an operation but couldn't save the king. This is how the hundredth tiger took its revenge upon the King.

**Explanation.** In Kalki's story the hundredth tiger is not a real one: the Maharaja had bought the wooden toy from a shop in Pratibandapuram, and it was carved badly, with tiny slivers of wood standing up on its surface. The prophecy promised death "from the tiger", and a toy tiger fulfils it exactly — which is the story's final joke at the expense of a lifetime of hunting.

questions.question: What did Dr. Sadao and his wife do with the American soldier? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Dr. Sadao Hoki was a Japanese doctor at the coast and a renowned scientist who had specially mastered the art of healing wounds. One night he and his good wife Hana saw a man crawling out of the mist and falling on his face. They found he was a **badly wounded white man, an enemy soldier from the US Navy**. They were in a dilemma: first they thought of throwing him back into the sea, but since he was wounded and unconscious their compassionate nature could not allow them to ignore him, so they **took him inside**.

Hana herself washed him with warm water as her maid refused to do so. **Dr. Sadao operated upon the deep wound and pulled the bullet out** from the bleeding wound. He gave him an injection and Hana administered anaesthesia to him. Their servants had left the house in protest, yet they nursed and looked after him till he felt fully fit and recovered. After much thought Dr. Sadao decided to **send the soldier to the unguarded island in the sea**: he gave him his boat, clothes, food, water and his flashlight, and instructed him to wait for only the Korean fishing boat to go away. Finally Dr. Sadao felt relieved, rewarded and happy when there was no flash of light by sunset, which meant that the prisoner had gone from the island — safe and well.

questions.question: Why did Roger Skunk go to visit the owl? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** A skunk is a small black and white American animal. **Roger Skunk was a little animal that smelled very badly.** His bad smell kept all other little animals away from him; they never played with him. He stood all alone, **weeping over his fate**, and so he went to the wise old owl for advice.

**Explanation.** In "Should Wizard Hit Mommy?" (a chapter now outside the current syllabus) the owl sends Roger to the wizard, who charges seven pennies and makes him smell like a rose. Roger is happy, but his mother is not: she takes him back and makes the wizard restore his skunk smell, because "he is a skunk and he must smell like one". Jack's refusal to let the mother be punished is what upsets his daughter Jo.

questions.chapter: Journey to the End of the Earth
questions.question: What happened to Gondwana 150 million years ago? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Gondwana prospered for **500 million years**. But around this time the **dinosaurs were wiped out**; the age of the mammals started; the landmass was **forced to separate into countries**. India was pushed northwards and the **Himalayas were formed**. This disruption shaped the globe much as we know it today.

**Explanation.** In Tishani Doshi's "Journey to the End of the Earth" Gondwana is the southern supercontinent that once joined India, Antarctica, Africa, South America and Australia. Its break-up explains the position of the continents, the rise of the Himalayas and the climate that Antarctica's ice cores now record.

questions.question: Why does Mr. Lamb have a tin leg? (Answer in about 35 words.)
questions.answer:
**Answer.** Mr. Lamb has a **tin leg** because **one of his legs was blown off in the war**. He has to walk on an artificial tin leg. But Mr. Lamb doesn't feel like a physically handicapped person, nor does he suffer from an inferiority complex. Children call him "Lamey-Lamb", but he doesn't mind it.

**Explanation.** In Susan Hill's play Mr. Lamb's own disability is what makes him able to talk to Derry, whose face was burnt by acid. When Derry says people are afraid of his face, Lamb replies that he is afraid of nothing in his garden — "it's all relative". His tin leg is thus not a complaint but an argument.
